orient: Narrator: Mr. Lockwood, writing in his diary in 1801. He is a gentleman from the south of England who has just rented a house in the remote Yorkshire moors, and this entry describes his first visit to his landlord.

notes.g: The year of Lockwood's diary entry.
notes.n: The book opens in the 'present' of 1801. Much of what you will hear later happened decades earlier, so it helps to keep this date in mind.

notes.g: The man who owns the house Lockwood is renting.
notes.m: Not an innkeeper or pub owner.

notes.t: solitary neighbour that I shall be troubled with
notes.g: The only neighbour I'll have to deal with.
notes.n: Lockwood is being playful: he likes the idea of having almost no neighbours.

notes.g: Beautiful countryside or region.
notes.m: 'Country' here means landscape or district, not a nation.

notes.g: Chosen a place to live.
notes.m: 'Situation' means location or site, not circumstances.

notes.g: The busy social life of towns and polite company.
A person who dislikes and avoids other people.
notes.n: Today we usually say 'misanthrope'. Lockwood calls the place a hater-of-people's paradise.

notes.g: An excellent man; a first-rate chap.
notes.m: 'Capital' as an adjective meant 'excellent', with nothing to do with money or cities.

notes.g: Saw; looked at.
A sleeveless garment worn over a shirt and under a coat.
notes.n: In American English, a vest. Heathcliff hides his hands in it to avoid shaking hands.

notes.t: I do myself the honour of calling
notes.g: I am paying you a visit (very formal).
notes.n: To 'call' on someone was to make a polite social visit.

notes.g: My persistence in asking to rent (the house).
notes.n: Lockwood's speech is wordy and over-polite, which contrasts with Heathcliff's blunt replies.

notes.g: The house Lockwood has rented from Heathcliff, about four miles from Wuthering Heights.
notes.n: A 'grange' is a country house with farm buildings. It sits lower down, in a sheltered valley.

notes.g: Prevent; stop.
Go to the devil! Get lost!
notes.n: 'The Deuce' was a mild way of saying 'the devil'. The phrase is what Heathcliff's tone meant, not what he said.

notes.g: Leaned (British past tense).
Showed no sign of moving in agreement.
notes.n: A joke: even the gate stayed shut, as unwelcoming as its owner.

notes.g: Made me decide.
notes.m: Here 'determine' is used with a person as the object, meaning 'caused me to resolve'.

notes.g: Extremely private and unwilling to show feelings.
Actually pushing; fully pressing against.
notes.m: 'Fairly' means 'completely' or 'actually' here, not 'somewhat'.

notes.g: In a gloomy, resentful, silent way.
Walked ahead of.
A raised, paved path, here running up to the house.
notes.n: In the wet moorland country, farm paths were often paved with stones and raised above the mud.

notes.g: Entered the courtyard: the enclosed yard in front of the farmhouse.
The household staff of servants.
notes.m: 'Domestics' means servants, not something to do with home life in general.
notes.n: Lockwood jokes that one old servant seems to be the whole staff.

notes.g: A two-part order (take the horse, and bring wine).
Flagstones: the flat paving stones of the yard.
notes.m: Not flags as in banners.
notes.n: Grass growing between them is a sign the place is neglected.

notes.g: Nobody trims the hedges; only the cattle eating them keep them short.
notes.n: Another sign of a poorly kept farm.

notes.g: No, rather; or even.
notes.n: Used to correct yourself with a stronger word: 'elderly, no, actually old'.

notes.g: Healthy and strong, lean and muscular.
Talked to himself.
notes.n: From 'soliloquy', a speech made alone, as in a play.

notes.g: Irritable, grumpy.
Kindly guessed (giving him the benefit of the doubt).
Help from God.
The main meal of the day, eaten around midday.
notes.m: In the rural north in 1801, 'dinner' was a midday meal, not an evening one.

notes.g: A short, sudden religious exclamation.
notes.m: 'Ejaculation' meant any short burst of speech, especially a quick prayer like 'The Lord help us!'. It had no sexual meaning here.
notes.n: 'Pious' means religious or devout. Joseph is very religious, in a harsh way.

notes.g: Arrival.
Heathcliff's house: an old farmhouse high up on the exposed moors.
notes.n: 'Heights' means high ground. The title of the book is the name of this house.

notes.g: A Yorkshire word for the roaring, blustering sound and force of a strong wind.
notes.n: Related to the dialect verb 'to wuther', to blow fiercely. Lockwood explains it himself in the next words.

notes.g: A local, regional word, not standard English.
notes.n: 'Provincial' means belonging to the provinces, far from London.

notes.g: Wild, stormy weather.
notes.n: Lockwood likes fancy phrases for simple things.

notes.g: Its position or location.
notes.m: Nothing to do with trains.

notes.g: Refreshingly cold, strong fresh air.
notes.n: A wry joke: the house is extremely windy.

notes.g: Over the brow or ridge of the hill above the house.
Small, poorly grown fir trees, kept short by the wind.
Thin, bare hawthorn trees.
notes.n: Hawthorn is a tough thorny tree common in northern hedges and hillsides.

notes.g: Begging the sun for charity.
notes.n: 'Alms' are money or food given to the poor. The bent trees look like beggars reaching out their arms.

notes.g: Fantastical decorative carving mixing human, animal and imaginary figures.
notes.m: In art, 'grotesque' names a decorative style. It doesn't just mean 'ugly'.

notes.g: Spread generously; used in great quantity.
Mythical creatures with a lion's body and an eagle's head and wings.
Carvings of naked cherubs or little boys.
notes.n: 'Shameless' because they are naked; Lockwood is being humorous.

notes.g: The name carved over the door with the date 1500, probably of the man who built the house.
notes.n: Earnshaw is the old family name linked to Wuthering Heights. Keep this name in mind.

notes.g: Rude and bad-tempered.
Make worse.
notes.m: Its older, stricter sense: 'make more serious', rather than just 'annoy'.

notes.g: Before.
The innermost part of a building; its most private rooms.
notes.n: From the Latin 'penetralia'. Lockwood uses a showy Latin word to sound clever.

notes.g: An entrance hall.
In Yorkshire farmhouses, 'the house' was the name for the main living room.
notes.n: 'Pre-eminently' means 'above all else': this room is called 'the house' as if it were the whole home.

notes.g: A sitting room, often a tidier one for receiving visitors.
Cooking pots and tools.
Colanders: bowls with holes for draining food.
notes.n: An old spelling.

notes.g: A dull grey metal (mainly tin) used for plates, dishes and mugs.
Large metal drinking mugs with handles, often with lids.
A tall kitchen cupboard with open shelves on top for displaying plates and dishes.
notes.m: Not a bedroom chest of drawers (the American sense).

notes.g: Given a ceiling.
notes.n: The room has no plaster ceiling, so you can see the bare roof beams ('its entire anatomy').

notes.g: Thin, flat cakes made of oatmeal, a staple food in northern England.
notes.n: They were hung on a wooden rack near the ceiling to dry.

notes.g: Meat from a grown sheep.
notes.n: The legs of meat hanging from the ceiling are being cured and stored.

notes.g: Various; several.
Nasty-looking, wicked-looking (said playfully).
Large pistols carried in holsters on a horse's saddle.
In a bright, showy, tasteless way.
Small containers with lids, such as tea tins.
Arranged along.
notes.m: 'Disposed' means placed or set out, not thrown away.

notes.g: Simple, roughly made things (here, chairs).
A reddish-brown female hunting dog.
notes.n: 'Liver' is a reddish-brown dog colour. 'Bitch' was the ordinary word for a female dog. A pointer is a breed that stands still and 'points' at game birds.

notes.g: Plain, simple, unpretentious.
notes.m: In British English this is a kind word. In American English it now means 'unattractive'.

notes.g: Face, or the expression on it.
Strong and sturdy.
Trousers that end just below the knee, fastened there.
notes.n: Old-fashioned working dress for a farmer by 1801.

notes.g: Coverings of leather or cloth for the lower leg and ankle, worn to keep off mud.
A striking, remarkable contrast.
notes.m: 'Singular' means unusual or remarkable, not 'one'.

notes.g: Home; dwelling place.
An old spelling of 'Gypsy', a term for the Romani people.
notes.n: The word is now often considered offensive. Brontë uses it to mark Heathcliff's dark appearance and his status as an outsider, which becomes very important in the story.

notes.g: The main landowner in a country district; a gentleman farmer.
Untidy, careless about appearance.
Not looking bad; looking fine.
notes.n: His careless clothes suit him.

notes.g: Gloomy and unsociable.
Badly brought up; lacking good manners and breeding.
A feeling of kinship; something in me that resonates with him.
notes.n: Lockwood believes he and Heathcliff are alike. The reader soon learns how wrong he is.

notes.g: A strong dislike.

notes.t: esteem it a species of impertinence
notes.g: Consider it a kind of rudeness.
notes.m: 'Esteem' means 'judge, consider'; 'species' means 'kind or type'.

notes.g: Loved or hated back, in return.
notes.m: 'Again' here means 'in return', not 'one more time'.

notes.g: Getting carried away; jumping to conclusions.
Give him too many of my own qualities.
notes.n: In other words, Lockwood admits he is projecting himself onto Heathcliff.

notes.g: Motivate; drive (someone to act).
Personal temperament; the way a person is made.
notes.m: Not a set of laws.

notes.g: Particular; special to one person or thing.
notes.m: Often means 'belonging specifically to' rather than 'strange'.

notes.g: Happened to spend time with.
A charming person (here, a young woman).
notes.m: 'Creature' was an affectionate word for a person, not an animal.

notes.g: A quotation from Shakespeare's Twelfth Night.
notes.n: In the play, Viola describes someone who 'never told her love' and suffered in silence. Lockwood dresses up his cowardice in literary language.

notes.g: Completely (in love); head over heels.
Gave him a loving look back.
Leave suddenly.
Quirk of personality.
The flat stone floor in front of and under the fireplace.
The mother dog (Lockwood's fancy phrasing).
A quick bite.
A snarl or growl.
At the same time, in the same way.
notes.n: A joke: Heathcliff growls along with his dog.

notes.g: A sign or hint.
French: face to face with.
Thuggish, violent.
Silent insults (made with faces, not words).
Face; facial expression.
notes.n: Physiognomy was also the popular idea that character could be read from the face.

notes.g: The female dog, given a mock-polite title.
Put (something) between.
Devils; demons.
The tails or lower flaps of a coat.
Fending off, blocking (a term from sword fighting).
Effectively.
A metal rod for stirring a fire.
Forced.
Infuriating calmness.
notes.m: 'Phlegm' here means a slow, unexcitable temperament (from the old theory of the four 'humours'), not mucus. 'Vexatious' means annoying.

notes.g: Dogs biting, shaking and attacking.
notes.m: To 'worry' was what a dog does to sheep or prey: seize and tear at it. Not feeling anxious.

notes.g: Moved more quickly.
notes.n: 'Dispatch' means speed.

notes.g: A strong, vigorous woman.
notes.m: 'Lusty' meant healthy and energetic, not lustful. 'Dame' just means a woman.

notes.g: Dress or skirt pinned up out of the way for work.
So effectively.
A reference to the Bible.
notes.n: In the Gospels (Mark 5, Matthew 8), Jesus drives devils out of a man and into a herd of pigs, which then rush into the sea. Lockwood is answering Heathcliff's 'What the devil?'

notes.g: A family of young tigers.
Interfere; bother (someone).
Watchful, on guard.

notes.t: set my signet on the biter
notes.g: Left my mark on the biter (that is, hit back).
notes.n: A signet is a seal pressed into wax to stamp a mark. Lockwood means he would have struck the dog.

notes.g: Flustered, agitated.
Willing to admit.
notes.m: 'Own' as a verb here means 'confess', not 'possess'.

notes.g: Drank to his health in return.
notes.n: A 'pledge' was a toast.

notes.g: Mongrel dogs; worthless dogs.
Unwilling, reluctant (now spelled 'loath').
That was the kind of mood he was in.
notes.m: 'Humour' means mood or temper here, not comedy.

notes.g: Careful, practical thought about his own interests.
Using very few words; terse.

notes.t: chipping off his pronouns and auxiliary verbs
notes.g: Speaking in clipped phrases.
notes.n: For example 'Not bitten, are you?' and 'Take a glass of wine?' instead of full sentences.

notes.g: A conversation or talk on a subject.
Place of retreat, away from society.
notes.m: Not retirement from work. Lockwood means a quiet hideaway.

notes.g: Tomorrow (older hyphenated spelling).
All the same; nevertheless.
Lockwood's landlord. He owns Thrushcross Grange but lives at Wuthering Heights.
notes.n: The central figure of the novel. Watch how differently Lockwood and others see him.

notes.g: The narrator: Heathcliff's new tenant at Thrushcross Grange.
notes.n: A fashionable gentleman who thinks himself shy and deep. He is often comically wrong about people.

notes.g: Heathcliff's elderly servant.
notes.n: Joseph is grimly religious and speaks broad Yorkshire dialect, which gets much thicker in later chapters.
